## The presenters

Rebecca Fisher, Australian Institute of Marine Science.

This course will focus on the `bayesnec` R the package developed at AIMS by Myself and
Diego Barneche. It is described in *Journal of Statistical Software*
110(5).

XX ADD screenshot Fisher_etal2024_JSS.png XX



Helpers are in the room during the sessions where you run the code. Put a hand
up and one will come to you rather than waiting until the break.

::: {.notes}
Fifteen minutes for this block, 10:00 to 10:15. Module 1 starts at 10:15.
:::

## The shape of the day

| Time | |
|---|---|
| 10:00 | Welcome, and an introduction to concentration-response modelling |
| 10:15 | The software stack, and fitting your first model in `bayesnec` |
| 12:30 | Lunch, served one level below |
| 13:15 | Toxicity estimates, model averaging, and choosing a statistical distribution |
| 14:30 | Break. Coffee, tea and snacks in Room 301. |
| 14:45 | Priors, and a worked case study from start to finish |
| 16:00 | Finish |

Coffee and tea are next door in Room 301. The day ends at 16:00, in time for the
conference opening ceremony at 16:30.

## The outcomes

By the end of the day you will be able to:

- distinguish linear, non-linear and threshold concentration-response models,
  and say which suits a given endpoint;
- identify the statistical distribution appropriate to a response variable;
- fit concentration-response models in R and plot the results;
- derive NEC, NSEC and ECx estimates, and explain what each measures;
- apply model averaging across a candidate set, and interpret the weights;
- produce a complete workflow for estimating no-effect toxicity, suitable for
  use in a species sensitivity distribution.

## Concentration-response data


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](opening_files/figure-revealjs/fig-crdata-1.png){#fig-crdata fig-align='center' width=768}
:::
:::


An exposure across a concentration series, with a measured response at each
concentration. The response falls as concentration rises, and the question is
where it begins to fall and by how much.

## Estimates read from a fitted curve

Four quantities are in use, and they measure different things.

- The **NEC** is the concentration at which the response begins to decline. It
  is a parameter of a threshold model, estimated directly.
- The **NSEC** is the concentration at which the fitted curve crosses a lower
  quantile of the control response. It is defined for a smooth curve, which has
  no threshold to estimate.
- An **ECx** is the concentration producing an x per cent change from the
  control, most often EC10 or EC50.
- The **NOEC** is the highest test concentration whose treatment mean is not
  statistically distinguishable from the control.

Module 3 takes each of these on a fitted curve.

## The place of a no-effect estimate

A no-effect estimate for each of several species is what a species sensitivity
distribution is built from, and the distribution is what a guideline value is
derived from.

The estimate you report therefore propagates into the protective concentration
someone else calculates.

Warne et al. (2025), the current Australian and New Zealand method, lists the
NEC and the NSEC as the two most preferred statistical estimates of toxicity.

## The difficulty with the NOEC

The NOEC is one of the concentrations you happened to test, so it cannot fall
between two of them and it cannot be reported with an interval.

It also rewards an imprecise experiment. Wider variation makes a treatment
harder to distinguish from the control, which raises the concentration declared
to have no effect.

Fisher and Fox (2023) introduce the NSEC as the estimate that answers the same
question from a fitted curve.

## Fitting in a Bayesian framework

`bayesnec` fits these models through `brms` and Stan.

The fit returns a posterior distribution for every quantity, so an NEC, an NSEC
and an ECx each come with an interval without a separate calculation.

A prior is stated for each parameter. `bayesnec` sets weakly informative priors
from the data by default, and module 6 covers reading them and changing them.

## Model averaging

A candidate set of equations is fitted rather than one equation.

Each equation is weighted by how well it predicts, and the estimates are
averaged across the set by those weights.

The reason is that the equation is rarely known in advance, and a guideline
value derived from a single equation chosen after the fact omits the
uncertainty in that choice. Module 4 covers the weights and how to read them.

## The frequentist comparison

`drc` fits the same curves by maximum likelihood, and many people in this field
already use it.

It is supplied as a reference page rather than taught, and it is explicit about
where the two engines answer the same question and where they do not.

## The page and the teaching modes

The page on the projector is the page on your own screen, and each module shows
the code that produced every result on it.

Three modes are used through the day:

- **hands-on**, where you run the code as it is introduced;
- **demonstration**, where you watch it run and have the script to run later;
- **walk-through**, where the page is read and its output discussed.

## Fits that are loaded rather than sampled

A single model takes minutes to fit and a model-averaged set takes longer, so
nothing is sampled from scratch in the room.

Every fit appears as three steps: the `bnec()` call, the `save()` that keeps the
result, and the `load()` that reads it back. The call and the save are shown;
the load is what runs.

The saved objects are the download named in the setup instructions, and they are
on the USB sticks at the front. That sequence is what a real analysis does,
which is why it is on the page rather than hidden.

## A broken installation

You will be able to follow every demonstration, and the material stays online
afterwards.

Bring your laptop to a helper during a break rather than during a session, and
run `check_setup.R` first so that the output is in front of us.

Nothing is installed or repaired during teaching time; there is no slot for it
in the day.

## The material

<https://open-aims.github.io/cr_modelling_training/>

The site stays available after the workshop, and the source is at
<https://github.com/open-AIMS/cr_modelling_training>.

Corrections and questions are welcome as issues on that repository, including
after today.

## Module 1, the software stack

What R, Stan, `brms` and `bayesnec` each contribute, and how they fit together.
